displayQuote: By failing to prepare, you are preparing to fail

meta.title: Who really said "By failing to prepare, you are preparing to fail"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: No — Benjamin Franklin never said it. It is an anonymous proverb first documented in 1919, decades after his death, and only pinned on Franklin from 1970 on.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'By failing to prepare, you are preparing to fail'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Franklin. An anonymous proverb, earliest traced to 1919 (Rev. H. K. Williams); the Franklin credit is a later invention.

answer.label: Not Benjamin Franklin — an anonymous modern proverb
answer.sourceLine: There is no evidence Benjamin Franklin ever said or wrote this. It does not appear in his collected papers, and the earliest known version — “if you fail to prepare you are preparing to fail” — was printed in 1919, 129 years after Franklin’s death. Quote Investigator ↗ classifies it as an anonymous proverb, and the Check Your Fact ↗ ruling on the Franklin credit is “False.”

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: Remember, if you fail to prepare you are preparing to fail.
trail: 1919 — earliest known instance. Rev. H. K. Williams writes “if you fail to prepare you are preparing to fail” in The Biblical World, per Quote Investigator ↗.
1929 & 1977 — the proverb keeps circulating. S.C. education official James H. Hope used it in 1929, and coach John Wooden in 1977 — none crediting Franklin, per QI ↗.
1970 — the Franklin myth begins. A filler item in the Minneapolis Tribune first pins the line on Franklin, an ascription fact-checkers rate “False” ↗.
Proverb, not Franklin. The Dictionary of Modern Proverbs (Yale, 2012) lists it as anonymous proverbial wisdom, per QI ↗.
source.excerptNote: The earliest documented form, written by Reverend H. K. Williams in The Biblical World (1919) — advice to those giving religious talks. The now-standard wording “By failing to prepare, you are preparing to fail” is a later, smoothed-out variant of this anonymous saying.

source.rightsNote: The exact popular wording is an anonymous proverb with no identifiable author or single source work, so no copyright status can be responsibly asserted. The earliest documented variant (1919) is itself old, but the line is not attributable to a specific rights-holding author.

author.name: Benjamin Franklin
author.heading: About Benjamin Franklin
author.metaLine: 1706–1790 · American statesman, printer & author of Poor Richard’s Almanack
author.bio: Benjamin Franklin was a founding father, printer, scientist and author whose Poor Richard’s Almanack (1732–1758) filled American memory with pithy maxims like “Well done is better than well said.” Precisely because he is the archetypal source of homespun American wisdom, he has become a “quote magnet” — countless anonymous sayings get pinned on him. This preparation adage is one of them: it appears nowhere in his genuine writings.

misattribution.heading: How Franklin got the credit
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook “quote magnet” misattribution: an anonymous proverb attached to a famous name long after the fact.

items.why: No record of the saying exists in Franklin’s collected writings or letters, and Franklin scholar Blaine McCormick notes it does not even “sound Colonial,” per Check Your Fact ↗. The credit first surfaces in a 1970 newspaper filler, per Quote Investigator ↗.
The UCLA coach used “When you fail to prepare, you’re preparing to fail” in 1977, helping spread it, but the saying predates him by decades, per Quote Investigator ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The real origin is an anonymous proverb, first documented in Rev. H. K. Williams’s 1919 wording in The Biblical World and catalogued as proverbial in the Dictionary of Modern Proverbs via QI ↗.

context.heading: Why this one sticks to Franklin
lead: Franklin’s Poor Richard’s Almanack made him America’s patron saint of practical maxims, so any crisp piece of self-improvement advice with a lost author tends to drift toward his name. The preparation proverb fits the mold perfectly — short, motivational, and morally tidy.

But the paper trail runs the other way: the line is documented only from 1919 onward, moved through educators and coaches as common-stock wisdom, and was not tied to Franklin until 1970 — the signature of an invented attribution rather than a lost quotation.
context.pull: An anonymous proverb wearing a founding father’s coat.
